title: Idempotency and retries
story:
A call across a network can fail after the work was done and before the answer arrived. That single fact is what this lesson is about, because it means the caller cannot distinguish work that never happened from work whose confirmation was lost — and those two situations call for opposite responses.

The protocol defines the property that resolves it. A request method is idempotent if the intended effect on the server of multiple identical requests with that method is the same as the effect for a single such request, and of the methods the specification defines, replacing a resource, deleting one, and the safe methods are idempotent. Note the phrasing: the intended effect. Not the response, and not the server's internal bookkeeping.

The specification then says exactly why the property is worth having. Idempotent methods are distinguished because the request can be repeated automatically if a communication failure occurs before the client is able to read the server's response. If a client sends such a request and the connection closes before any response is received, it can establish a new connection and retry, knowing that repeating the request will have the same intended effect even if the original succeeded — though the response might differ. That parenthetical matters: deleting an already-deleted thing may report differently the second time while leaving the same state behind, and the state is what idempotency is about.

The prohibition is equally explicit. A client should not automatically retry a request with a non-idempotent method unless it has some means to know that the request semantics are actually idempotent regardless of the method, or some means to detect that the original request was never applied. The specification observes drily that some clients take a riskier approach and attempt to guess when an automatic retry is possible. If you have ever been charged twice, you have met the result.

Which is where the design work is, because most operations that matter are not naturally repeatable. Creating an order, sending a message, moving money — each is a new fact every time it is performed. The standard construction is to have the caller supply a key identifying the attempt, and the server record which keys it has already applied, so a repeat is recognised and answered with the original outcome rather than performed again. That converts a non-repeatable operation into a repeatable one at the cost of remembering keys, which means deciding how long to remember them and what happens to a retry that arrives after you forgot.

One boundary worth keeping straight: the property is about intent rather than side effects. Like the definition of safe, it only applies to what has been requested by the user; a server is free to log each request separately, retain a revision history, or implement other non-idempotent side effects for each idempotent request.

problem.name: Idempotent operations
problem.shape: A request may fail after the work was performed and before the confirmation arrived, leaving the caller unable to tell which happened.
tell: a client retries automatically on timeout
an operation creates something new each time it runs
a duplicate record appears after a network incident
a retry policy exists and nobody has checked which methods it applies to
problem.move: Make operations repeatable before making clients retry. Where the operation is naturally repeatable, say so and allow automatic retry. Where it is not, have the caller supply a key identifying the attempt and record applied keys so a repeat returns the original outcome, then decide explicitly how long those keys are retained.
problem.invariant: An operation is idempotent when the intended effect of many identical requests equals the effect of one. The property concerns intended effect on state, not the response returned and not the server's incidental bookkeeping.
problem.breaks: Idempotency keys move the problem rather than removing it: the server must now remember which keys it has applied, for some finite period, and a retry arriving after that period is indistinguishable from a new request. So exactly-once becomes at-most-once within a retention window, which is a weaker and more honest claim.

cost.time: a lookup of the attempt key on every write path
cost.space: stored keys and their outcomes, for as long as a retry might plausibly arrive
cost.beats: retrying blindly, which duplicates work, and never retrying, which turns every transient failure into a user-visible one

worked.problem: Is it safe to retry a request that received no response?
worked.reasoning:
Only if the operation is idempotent — and the whole difficulty is that no response is exactly the case where you cannot tell whether it already happened.

Set out the situation precisely. The request went out. Either it never arrived, or it arrived and failed, or it arrived and succeeded and the response was lost. Those three are indistinguishable from the caller's side, and in the third the work is already done. So retrying is safe only when doing the work twice is equivalent to doing it once.

That is what the definition provides: a method is idempotent if the intended effect on the server of multiple identical requests is the same as the effect for a single such request. The specification lists replacement, deletion and the safe methods as idempotent among those it defines, and says directly why the property earns its place — such a request can be repeated automatically if a communication failure occurs before the client is able to read the response. It gives the exact scenario: connection closed before any response, client opens a new connection and retries, knowing the intended effect is the same even if the original succeeded, though the response might differ.

I would emphasise that last clause, because it is where people get confused. Deleting something already deleted may return a different code the second time. That does not break idempotency, because the property is about the resulting state rather than the reply.

The prohibition is stated just as clearly: a client should not automatically retry a non-idempotent method unless it has some means to know the semantics are actually idempotent regardless of method, or some means to detect that the original was never applied. And the specification notes that some clients take a riskier approach and guess. Double charges are what guessing looks like from the outside.

So for operations that are not naturally repeatable — creating an order, sending a message, moving money — the answer is to make them repeatable rather than to avoid retrying. The construction is an attempt key supplied by the caller and recorded by the server, so that a repeat is recognised and answered with the original outcome instead of performed again.

And the honest caveat I would add, because it is usually skipped: that does not achieve exactly-once. The server remembers keys for a finite time, and a retry arriving after the retention window looks like a new request. What you actually get is at-most-once within a window, and choosing that window is a real decision rather than a detail.

problem.practice: Find your retry policy and list which operations it can fire on. For each one that creates or moves something, work out what two executions would produce. Then check whether any of them accepts an attempt key — and if so, how long the server remembers it.

beats.broke: A call across a network can fail after the work was done but before the answer arrives, so the caller cannot distinguish work that did not happen from work whose confirmation was lost.
beats.fix: Make the operation produce the same intended effect whether performed once or many times, so retrying an unanswered request is safe without knowing which case occurred.
beats.cost: The property has to be designed in — usually by having the caller supply a key identifying the attempt — because most operations that matter are not naturally repeatable, and the server must then remember keys it has seen.

interview.q: Is it safe to retry a request that received no response?
interview.trap: Answering yes for reads and no for writes. The distinction is idempotency rather than reading or writing — a replacement is a write and is safely repeatable — and the honest caveat is that attempt keys give at-most-once within a retention window, not exactly-once.
interview.answer:
Only if the operation is idempotent — and the difficulty is that no response is exactly the case where you cannot tell whether it already happened.

Three possibilities are indistinguishable from the caller: it never arrived, it arrived and failed, or it arrived and succeeded and the response was lost. In the third the work is already done, so retrying is safe only when doing it twice equals doing it once.

That is the definition: a method is idempotent if the intended effect on the server of multiple identical requests is the same as the effect for a single one. The specification lists replacement, deletion and the safe methods among those it defines, and says why it matters — such a request can be repeated automatically if a communication failure occurs before the client can read the response, so a client whose connection closed can reconnect and retry knowing the intended effect is the same even if the original succeeded, though the response might differ.

That last clause is where people get confused: deleting an already-deleted thing may return a different code the second time, which does not break idempotency, because the property concerns resulting state rather than the reply.

The prohibition is equally explicit — a client should not automatically retry a non-idempotent method unless it knows the semantics are idempotent regardless of method, or can detect the original was never applied. The specification notes some clients guess instead; double charges are what guessing looks like from outside.

So for operations that are not naturally repeatable — creating an order, moving money — make them repeatable rather than avoid retrying, via an attempt key supplied by the caller and recorded by the server so a repeat returns the original outcome.

The caveat I would add is that this is not exactly-once. Keys are remembered for a finite time, and a retry arriving later looks like a new request — so what you get is at-most-once within a window, and choosing that window is a real decision.

MAKING THE UNREPEATABLE REPEATABLE

   caller supplies an ATTEMPT KEY
   server records APPLIED keys
   a repeat returns the ORIGINAL OUTCOME

THE CAVEAT NOBODY MENTIONS

   this is NOT exactly-once.

takeaway: A lost response is indistinguishable from work that never happened, so retrying is safe only when the intended effect of many requests equals that of one — and attempt keys buy you at-most-once within a retention window rather than exactly-once.
